intro.heading: The paperwork is complete. The picture is not.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A care home manager welcomes three new carers who have just arrived from abroad. The first week goes well. Policies are shown, the tour is done, the induction booklet is signed. Everyone is keen and polite, and in group briefings the three nod along. By week three the manager notices small things: a question about the safeguarding lead that gets a hesitant answer, a medication policy that was marked as read in two minutes. Nobody has been careless. The manager simply has a signature for each person and no way to see what is understood. Here is how it plays out.

trail.text: A warm welcome at the door and a tour with a colleague in a lanyard.
Three new starters are given the policy pack and the induction booklet.
All three sign the induction sheet. Everyone is positive.
The group briefing moves fast, and the new starters nod rather than ask.
The medication policy is marked as read in two minutes by one carer.
A carer cannot say who the safeguarding lead is, and is too polite to say so.
Three signatures. Nothing that shows what each person understood.
“What did your induction cover, and how do you know it worked?”

trail_close: The welcome was never the problem. The gap is between a signed induction and a team member you know has understood it. Here is how CareStream fills that gap using your own policies.

why.heading: A signature shows the policy was handed over, not understood
why.sub: The aim is simple. A wrong answer should show a knowledge gap, never a word gap.

cards.title: Language barriers in healthcare cut both ways
cards.body: New starters often understand more than they say. Others read policy English that was written for managers, not learners. Language barriers in healthcare settings are easy to miss in a busy first week.

cards.title: Skill and language are different things
cards.body: A carer may know exactly what to do and still stumble on a policy phrase. A check in their own language tells you which it is, so you do not guess.

cards.title: Quiet nods hide gaps
cards.body: Polite staff rarely say they have not followed. Without a short knowledge check, a gap can sit unseen until a resident, a relative or a reviewer asks.

talk.heading: Questions managers ask us
talk.sub: Plain answers about onboarding overseas care workers with CareStream.

items.q: Our new starters read the policies in week one. What more could we do?
items.a: Reading is a start, and CareStream records that a policy was opened and marked as read. A knowledge check shows whether it was understood. Add short questions on the topics that matter most, built from your own policies.

items.q: Do the induction questions appear in their own language?
items.a: On the paid plans, yes. Your admin sets each person's first language, and policies, induction steps and questions appear in it. It is machine translation, not professional human translation, so we recommend you review key wording and use the translation glossary.

items.q: What if a carer prefers to read a step in English?
items.a: If your admin allows switching and sets a second language, a carer can flip one lesson, question set or induction step into the second language with a Read in button. The default stays their first language.

items.q: What happens when a new starter gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes into their Follow-up tab in the Staff Hub and they get an email, at most once a day, in English. They choose Learn & retry for a short lesson then a fresh question, or Just retry. They can retry as often as they need.

items.q: Does that mean I am told each time someone gets one wrong?
items.a: No. Nothing alerts you on each wrong answer. You see the pattern in Analytics, Knowledge gaps, and in a Monday digest email.

items.q: Will it tell me whether it was the words or the knowledge?
items.a: Not on its own. It shows which questions were missed and whether the carer used the lesson. Looking at the topic and the language setting, then having a conversation, tells you which it was.

items.q: Does it replace our induction or the Care Certificate?
items.a: No. Keep your welcome, shadow shifts and in person induction. CareStream adds checks of understanding. There is also a Care Certificate course staff can work through.

items.q: What does it cost, and can we try it?
items.a: There is a 14 day free trial on the paid plans. Create a free account at the register page, and see pricing for the plans. Adhoc training and translation are on the paid plans only.

limits.heading: A check on understanding, not a replacement for your induction

cards.title: It is not professional translation
cards.body: Translation is done by machine, with your glossary and any improvements your team suggests and you approve. It is good for reading and checking, but it is not certified. Review key wording if it matters.

cards.title: It does not tell you why an answer was wrong
cards.body: A missed question shows a gap. Whether it came from the topic or the wording is something you find out by talking to the carer, which is the right place for it.

cards.title: Adhoc training and translation are on paid plans
cards.body: Both come with the paid plans. The free plan is English only and does not include adhoc training. Hub menus and wrong answer emails are in English on every plan.

items.q: How can I tell if a new carer has understood their induction?
items.a: Ask them a few short questions on the topics that matter. A knowledge check built from your own policies, in the Staff Hub, does this without a meeting. The result is on their staff record.

items.q: How do I support English as a second language in induction?
items.a: Allow time, use plain wording and check understanding rather than assuming it. With CareStream on a paid plan, induction questions and policies show in a carer's first language, with a second language available on request.

items.q: Is training in other languages professionally translated?
items.a: No. It is machine translation by Claude, with your own glossary and any improvements your team suggests that an admin approves. Never treat it as certified translation.
Dozens of languages. See the languages page. Hub menus and buttons stay in English.

items.q: How are new starters put onto an induction flow?
items.a: They are enrolled automatically in the induction flow for their role. The staff record flags an induction not started after 7 days, so a missed start does not go unnoticed.

items.q: How do I reduce language barriers in healthcare teams when training?
items.a: Use plain wording, short lessons and a check of understanding rather than a long briefing. Translating the policies and questions helps. Our guide to translating care policies goes into more detail.

items.q: What do I see as the manager?
items.a: The Knowledge gaps view in Analytics, with open gaps, staff affected, closed in 30 days and most missed questions, plus a Monday digest email.

items.q: Does this cover the Care Certificate?
items.a: It supports it. The Care Certificate standards number 16, and our Care Certificate course covers them. Your own induction and observation still matter.

guide.heading: A practical first month for overseas care workers
guide.lede: Where there is a language difference, the aim is to make understanding visible early, kindly and without singling anyone out. Here is a way to plan it.

sections.h3: Plan the first weeks around understanding
paragraphs: The Care Certificate from Skills for Care has 16 standards, and Skills for Care says the standards can inform what is covered during induction. The regulations also ask providers to make sure staff receive appropriate support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal as is necessary for their duties.

So the question for week three is not whether the booklet was signed. It is whether the person can do the job safely and knows where to turn. Our four week induction playbook sets out a week by week plan, and you can read more on giving new staff access to policies.

sections.h3: A simple routine for each new starter
checklist: Set their first language, and a second if useful, before day one
Enrol them in induction and check the first step was started within a week
Add short knowledge checks on safeguarding, medication and reporting
Review the Knowledge gaps view and talk to anyone with open gaps by week three

paragraphs: A missed question is information, not a verdict. Tell new starters that wrong answers lead to a short lesson and that retries are unlimited. Where a gap persists, a short chat, a shadow shift or a supervision will tell you more than any score.

guide.note: CareStream adds checks of understanding. It does not replace shadowing, supervision or your own judgement of competence.
